name: Nirvana
kicker: Buddhism’s highest goal · The “blowing out” of craving and rebirth
briefing: Picture a candle flame going out: that is what the word nirvana means, a “blowing out.” Buddhists believe that greed, hatred, and delusion keep beings trapped in samsara, an endless cycle of birth, death, and rebirth, and that nirvana is the perfect peace that comes when those fires go out for good. According to tradition, Siddhartha Gautama reached it at about age 35, becoming the Buddha, and taught the Eightfold Path as the way there.
answerHtml: nirvana (or nibbana; accept parinirvana; prompt on enlightenment, awakening, bodhi, or liberation; do not accept “moksha,” “samsara,” or “satori”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In the Fire Sermon, the Buddha taught that the eyes, the ears, and even the mind are “burning” with the fires of greed, hatred, and delusion, and T. S. Eliot named part of his poem _The Waste Land_ after that sermon. This state is reached when those three fires go out for good.
tossups.r: Its name is often translated as “blowing out,” like a flame. For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhism, an escape from the cycle of rebirth.

tossups.p: At Kushinagar [“koo-shee-NAH-gar”] in India, the dying Buddha lay on his right side between two sal [“SAHL”] trees and told his monks, “All conditioned things pass away; strive on with diligence.” Giant reclining statues, like the one at Wat Pho [“waht POH”] in Bangkok, show him at the moment he entered the final form of this state.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of freedom from the cycle of rebirth, which Buddhists seek by following the Eightfold Path.

tossups.p: The philosopher Nagarjuna [“nah-GAR-joo-nuh”] argued that there is not the slightest difference between this state and samsara [“sum-SAH-ruh”], since both are “empty” of any fixed, independent existence. Nagarjuna founded the Middle Way, or Madhyamaka [“mahd-YAH-muh-kuh”], school of Mahayana Buddhism.
tossups.r: This state ends samsara, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. For 10 points, name this ultimate goal of Buddhism.

tossups.p: When the wanderer Vacchagotta [“VAH-chuh-GOHT-tuh”] asked where an enlightened person goes after death, the Buddha asked him which way a fire goes when it goes out, to show that the question did not fit. A person who reaches this state while alive is said to have no fuel left for another birth.
tossups.r: Its Sanskrit name means “blowing out,” like a candle flame. For 10 points, name this Buddhist state of perfect peace.

tossups.p: A truth called nirodha [“nih-ROH-dah”], or “cessation,” teaches that suffering and the craving behind it can come to a complete end, and this state is that ending. The Buddha first taught that truth, the third of four, in his first sermon in the Deer Park at Sarnath [“SAR-naht”].
tossups.r: Those teachings are the Four Noble Truths. For 10 points, name this goal of the Noble Eightfold Path.

tossups.p: Mahayana Buddhists honor bodhisattvas [“boh-dee-SAHT-vuhz”], such as Avalokiteshvara [“uh-vuh-loh-kih-TAYSH-vuh-ruh”], who put off their own final entry into this state in order to help all other beings reach it. In the Pure Land school, believers hope to be reborn in Amitabha’s [“uh-mee-TAH-buhz”] paradise, where reaching this state is easier.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Buddhist goal, often explained as the “blowing out” of craving.

tossups.p: Theravada Buddhism describes four stages on the way to this state, beginning with the “stream-enterer,” who is said to reach it within seven more lifetimes. The middle stages are the once-returner and the non-returner, and a person at the fourth stage, who has reached it, is called an arhat [“AR-hut”].
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state in which craving and suffering end, the ultimate goal of Buddhism.

tossups.p: Verses of the _Dhammapada_ [“DAH-muh-PAH-duh”] call this state “the highest happiness,” and another early text calls it “unborn, unmade, and unconditioned.” Unlike heaven in many religions, it is usually described not as a place but as a state of perfect peace that words cannot fully capture.
tossups.r: Buddhists believe it brings an end to rebirth. For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhism, whose name means “blowing out.”

tossups.p: Jains celebrate Diwali as the night when Mahavira [“muh-HAH-vee-ruh”], the last of their twenty-four great teachers, reached this state at Pawapuri [“PAH-vah-poo-ree”] in eastern India. Jains often call the soul’s final liberation moksha, but they use this word for Mahavira’s passing too.
tossups.r: In Buddhism, it is the goal of the Eightfold Path. For 10 points, name this state of liberation from rebirth.

tossups.p: Tibetan paintings of the Wheel of Life show a rooster, a snake, and a pig chasing each other at the center, standing for greed, hatred, and ignorance. The whole wheel, gripped by Yama [“YAH-muh”], the lord of death, stands for the cycle of rebirth, and a Buddha is often painted outside it, pointing the way to this state.
tossups.r: That cycle of rebirth is called samsara. For 10 points, name this Buddhist goal, which frees a person from samsara forever.

tossups.p: Some Buddhist texts describe two kinds of this state: one “with remainder,” reached by an enlightened person who is still alive, and one “without remainder,” reached at that person’s death, when the five aggregates [“AG-reh-gits”] that make up a living being fall away for good.
tossups.r: Siddhartha Gautama reached it while meditating under the Bodhi tree, becoming the Buddha. For 10 points, name this state, which ends suffering and rebirth.

tossups.p: In one parable, the Buddha compared his teachings to a raft that carries a traveler across a river to the safety of the far shore, and said the raft should be left behind once the crossing is done. Buddhist texts often call this state “the further shore.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhism, a state of perfect peace beyond the cycle of rebirth.

tossups.p: Theravada monks practice vipassana [“vih-PAH-suh-nuh”], or “insight” meditation, hoping to see clearly that nothing lasts and that there is no unchanging self, an insight said to lead to this state. Right mindfulness and right concentration are the last two steps of the path to it.
tossups.r: That path is the Noble Eightfold Path. For 10 points, name this Buddhist goal, an end to suffering and rebirth.

tossups.p: After the god Brahma Sahampati [“suh-HUM-puh-tee”] begged the newly awakened Buddha to teach, the Buddha agreed and declared that “the doors to the deathless” were open. “The deathless,” or amata [“uh-MUH-tuh”], is a name for this state, because one who reaches it will never be born or die again.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhism, whose name comes from a Sanskrit word for “blowing out.”

tossups.p: After eating a final meal served by a metalworker named Cunda [“CHOON-dah”], the eighty-year-old Buddha fell ill, but he told his followers that Cunda should not be blamed. Soon afterward, the Buddha died and entered the final, complete form of this state.
tossups.r: In everyday English, its name has come to mean any state of perfect happiness. For 10 points, name this goal of Buddhism.

clues.t: The ultimate goal of Buddhism: freedom from suffering and from samsara, the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth
Its Sanskrit name means “blowing out,” like a candle flame going out
Siddhartha Gautama reached it while meditating under the Bodhi tree and became the Buddha (“Awakened One”)
Reached by following the Noble Eightfold Path
The third Noble Truth (nirodha, “cessation”): suffering can end, and this state is its ending
Reached when the three fires (or poisons) of greed, hatred, and delusion go out
In Theravada Buddhism, a person who has reached it is called an arhat (“worthy one”)
Mahayana bodhisattvas put off their own final entry into it in order to help all beings
The Buddha entered its final, complete form when he died at Kushinagar, at about age 80
Described not as a place like heaven but as a state of perfect peace beyond words
The Fire Sermon says the senses are “burning”; T. S. Eliot named part of _The Waste Land_ after it
Nagarjuna, founder of the Madhyamaka school, said there is not the slightest difference between it and samsara
Asked by Vacchagotta where an enlightened person goes after death, the Buddha asked which way a fire goes when it goes out
Reclining Buddha statues (like Wat Pho’s in Bangkok) show him dying on his right side; last words: “strive on with diligence”
Four stages to it: stream-enterer (within seven lives), once-returner, non-returner, and arhat
The _Dhammapada_ calls it “the highest happiness”; another early text calls it “unborn, unmade, and unconditioned”
Jains celebrate Diwali as the night Mahavira reached it at Pawapuri (Jains also call the soul’s final liberation moksha)
Tibetan Wheel of Life: a rooster, snake, and pig stand for greed, hatred, and ignorance; a Buddha outside the wheel points the way out
Two kinds: “with remainder” (while still alive) and “without remainder” (at death, when the five aggregates fall away)
The raft parable: the teachings carry you to the “further shore,” a name for this state, and are then left behind
Vipassana (“insight”) meditation, right mindfulness, and right concentration lead toward it
Called amata, “the deathless”; after Brahma Sahampati begged him to teach, the Buddha said “the doors to the deathless” were open
The Buddha fell ill after a last meal from the metalworker Cunda, then died and entered its final form
Pure Land Buddhists hope to be reborn in Amitabha’s paradise, where reaching it is easier

trap.title: Nirvana, moksha, or satori?
trap.body: Nirvana tossups are packed with words that sound like answers. Enlightenment (bodhi, or “awakening”) is the insight the Buddha gained under the Bodhi tree, and it earns only a prompt here. Moksha is the Hindu and Jain word for liberation, samsara is the cycle of rebirth that nirvana ends, and satori is a Zen word for a moment of awakening; none of those is accepted.
trap.fix: If the question describes a “blowing out,” the end of the three fires, the third Noble Truth, or what arhats and bodhisattvas reach, say nirvana. If you are prompted after saying “enlightenment,” add “nirvana”; save moksha for Hindu questions about Brahman and the atman.
trap.line: Real answer line: nirvana (or nibbana; prompt on enlightenment or bodhi; do not accept “moksha” or “samsara”)
